vignette: The air in the market smells like burnt sugar and iron, though Arjun knows the scent is only in his head. It is twenty minutes past his usual commute hour when the first detonation rips through the station. He stands too close to the tiled pillar when the secondary blast throws him across the platform. Glass rains down like ground ice. He crawls through a tangle of luggage and screaming voices, his palm pressing against a stranger's neck, feeling a pulse that feels impossibly far away. He makes it out, but something inside him does not follow him through the turnstiles. In the weeks that follow, Arjun returns to his office, but the familiar weight of his briefcase feels like a lead blanket. He is a psychologist, a man who maps the architecture of trauma and watches others rebuild from it. He tells himself that knowledge is armor. He sits at his desk and opens the diagnostic manuals, tracing the criteria for acute stress as if clinical language can contain the shaking in his hands. Instead of grounding him, the terminology becomes a mirror. He notices the gap between the textbooks and his own nervous system. When a client mentions a car backfiring, Arjun's pen stops mid-sentence. He feels the ghost of heat against his skin, the sudden metallic taste of fear, and he has to excuse himself to the restroom just to breathe through the tight band across his chest. At home, the silence feels heavy. His wife, Priya, learns to walk softly, but she cannot walk lightly enough to avoid the flinch that runs through him when the dishwasher clicks off. He stops watching the news, stops taking the subway, stops going to the family gatherings where the familiar hum of Urdu and Hindi suddenly feels like a trigger. He tells himself it is a temporary recalibration, a necessary boundary. But the boundaries bleed. He cancels a workshop he co-facilitates, citing a sudden migraine. In truth, he cannot sit in a room with more than six people without calculating the exits, without mentally mapping which chair would give him the clearest view of the door. His training usually allows him to hold space for others' chaos; now, he finds himself emotionally hoarding his own, terrified that if he leans into it, he will fracture. Now, at thirty-seven, Arjun moves through his days with a quiet, exhausting precision. He sits across from me today with his shoulders rolled forward, his hands folded neatly over his knees, his eyes tracking the movement of the ceiling fan. When I ask him about the morning, he pauses, his gaze dropping to the rug, then snapping back to the door before he answers. He speaks in careful, measured sentences, the voice of a clinician who has spent years learning to steady himself on a page. But his thumb rubs repeatedly over his wedding band, and his breath hitches just slightly when the street below erupts in a sudden chorus of car horns. He does not look away from the windows. He never does. He is a man who has built a life on understanding the mind, now navigating a body that still sounds the alarm at shadows. The work continues, not as a cure, but as a slow, deliberate negotiation with the present, one careful breath at a time.
